_comment: v0.16.1: curated linear-algebra kernel set. The Linear Algebra field run (2026-07-03) proved the math shard was calculus-only: the genome linker resolved 0/14 lessons for a linear algebra course, which cascaded into no judgment, no citations, and junk source-finder fallbacks. Tier-1 consensus content (anchor: null), same contract as the lang contributed kernels.

aliases: solution set of a linear system

definition.text: A system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations in the same variables; a solution assigns a value to each variable so that every equation holds simultaneously.

facts.text: A linear system has exactly zero, one, or infinitely many solutions — never, for example, exactly two.
A system is consistent when at least one solution exists and inconsistent when no solution exists.
Every linear system can be represented compactly as an augmented matrix and solved by row reduction.

misconceptions.text: Every system of equations has a solution.
misconceptions.corrective: A system like x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 is inconsistent: the equations describe parallel lines that never meet.

misconceptions.text: If a system has more than one solution, it has some finite number of them.
misconceptions.corrective: Over the real numbers, once a linear system has two distinct solutions it has infinitely many, because the whole line through the two solutions solves the system.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: Row reduction transforms a matrix using elementary row operations (swap two rows, scale a row by a nonzero constant, add a multiple of one row to another) into an echelon form from which solutions can be read off.

facts.text: Elementary row operations do not change the solution set of the linear system the matrix represents.
The reduced row echelon form of a matrix is unique, although different sequences of row operations can reach it.
A pivot is the first nonzero entry of a row in echelon form; pivot positions determine which variables are basic and which are free.

misconceptions.text: Row operations change the solutions of the system.
misconceptions.corrective: Each elementary row operation is reversible and preserves the solution set — that is exactly why elimination is a valid solving method.

misconceptions.text: The columns with the largest numbers become pivot columns.
misconceptions.corrective: Pivot positions are determined by echelon structure during elimination, not by the size of the entries.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: Matrix operations combine rectangular arrays of numbers: addition and scalar multiplication act entrywise, while the matrix product AB is defined when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B.

facts.text: Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: AB and BA can differ, and one product may not even be defined.
The (i, j) entry of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.
Matrix multiplication is associative and distributes over addition, so algebraic manipulation is possible as long as factor order is preserved.

misconceptions.text: Matrix multiplication works entrywise, like addition.
misconceptions.corrective: The product AB combines rows of A with columns of B via dot products; the entrywise product is a different, rarely used operation.

misconceptions.text: AB = BA for matrices, as with numbers.
misconceptions.corrective: Order matters in matrix products; AB = BA only in special cases, such as when one factor is the identity or both are powers of the same matrix.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: An n-by-n matrix A is invertible when there is a matrix B with AB = BA = I; the inverse is unique, written A⁻¹, and exists exactly when A has n pivots (equivalently, nonzero determinant).

facts.text: Only square matrices can be invertible, and even square matrices fail to be invertible when their columns are linearly dependent.
If A is invertible, the system Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b for every right-hand side b.
The inverse of a product reverses the order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ when both inverses exist.

misconceptions.text: Every nonzero matrix has an inverse.
misconceptions.corrective: A square matrix with a zero determinant — for example one with two equal rows — is nonzero yet has no inverse.

misconceptions.text: (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹.
misconceptions.corrective: Undoing two composed operations requires reversing their order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: A vector space is a set of objects (vectors) with addition and scalar multiplication that satisfy closure, associativity, commutativity, identity, inverse, and distributivity axioms; R^n is the standard example.

facts.text: A vector space must contain a zero vector, and every vector must have an additive inverse.
Vector spaces need not consist of geometric arrows: polynomials, matrices, and functions form vector spaces under the usual operations.
Closure matters: a subset of a vector space fails to be a vector space in its own right if adding two members or scaling a member can leave the subset.

misconceptions.text: Vectors are always arrows in 2D or 3D space.
misconceptions.corrective: Anything satisfying the vector-space axioms is a vector — polynomials, matrices, and functions included; geometry is one model, not the definition.

misconceptions.text: Any subset of R^n is a vector space.
misconceptions.corrective: A subset must contain the zero vector and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; a line not through the origin fails all three.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: A subspace is a subset of a vector space that contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication; the span of a set of vectors — all their linear combinations — is always a subspace.

facts.text: The span of a set of vectors is the smallest subspace containing them.
The column space of a matrix A is the span of its columns and consists of exactly those b for which Ax = b is consistent.
The null space of A is the set of solutions of Ax = 0 and is a subspace of the domain.

misconceptions.text: Any line or plane in R^3 is a subspace.
misconceptions.corrective: Only lines and planes through the origin are subspaces; others miss the zero vector and are not closed under scaling.

misconceptions.text: The span of two vectors is always a plane.
misconceptions.corrective: If the two vectors are parallel (or one is zero), their span collapses to a line or a point; the span's dimension depends on independence.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: Vectors are linearly independent when the only linear combination equal to the zero vector uses all zero coefficients; a nontrivial combination equal to zero is a dependence relation.

facts.text: A set containing the zero vector is automatically linearly dependent.
A set of vectors is dependent exactly when some vector in it is a linear combination of the others.
The columns of a matrix A are independent exactly when Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution — that is, every column is a pivot column.

misconceptions.text: Independent means the vectors are different from each other.
misconceptions.corrective: Distinct vectors can still be dependent — (1, 0), (0, 1), and (1, 1) are pairwise different yet dependent; independence is about redundancy, not distinctness.

misconceptions.text: More vectors give more independence.
misconceptions.corrective: Any set of more than n vectors in R^n is automatically dependent; adding vectors can only create dependence, never remove it.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: A basis of a vector space is a linearly independent set that spans the space; every basis of a given space has the same number of vectors, and that common count is the space's dimension.

facts.text: Every vector in the space is a unique linear combination of basis vectors; the coefficients are its coordinates in that basis.
All bases of a finite-dimensional vector space contain the same number of vectors.
In R^n, any n independent vectors form a basis, and any spanning set of n vectors is automatically independent.

misconceptions.text: A vector space has only one basis.
misconceptions.corrective: Spaces have infinitely many bases — R^2 is spanned by the standard basis but equally by (1, 1) and (1, -1); only the SIZE of a basis is fixed.

misconceptions.text: Dimension is the number of vectors in the space.
misconceptions.corrective: Dimension counts basis vectors, not members; R^2 has infinitely many vectors but dimension 2.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: The determinant is a scalar computed from a square matrix that is nonzero exactly when the matrix is invertible; geometrically, its absolute value scales area or volume under the matrix's transformation.

facts.text: A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero.
The determinant of a product is the product of determinants: det(AB) = det(A)det(B).
Row operations affect the determinant predictably: swapping rows flips its sign, scaling a row scales it, and adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged.

misconceptions.text: det(A + B) = det(A) + det(B).
misconceptions.corrective: The determinant is multiplicative, not additive: det(AB) = det(A)det(B), but det(A + B) usually differs from det(A) + det(B).

misconceptions.text: A matrix with small entries has a small determinant, and a large determinant means a 'big' matrix.
misconceptions.corrective: The determinant measures invertibility and volume scaling, not entry size; a matrix of large numbers can have determinant zero.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: A linear transformation is a function T between vector spaces that preserves addition and scalar multiplication: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u); every linear map from R^n to R^m is multiplication by an m-by-n matrix.

facts.text: A linear transformation always sends the zero vector to the zero vector.
The matrix of a linear transformation has as its columns the images of the standard basis vectors.
Rotations about the origin, reflections across lines through the origin, and projections onto subspaces are linear; translation by a nonzero vector is not.

misconceptions.text: Any function given by a formula in x and y is linear.
misconceptions.corrective: f(x) = x + 1 and f(x) = x² both fail linearity; the graph passing through the origin AND preserving sums and scalar multiples is required.

misconceptions.text: Translation is a linear transformation.
misconceptions.corrective: Translating by a nonzero vector moves the origin, so it violates T(0) = 0; translations are affine, not linear.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: An eigenvector of a square matrix A is a nonzero vector x whose image Ax is a scalar multiple of itself, Ax = λx; the scalar λ is the eigenvalue, found as a root of the characteristic polynomial det(A − λI).

facts.text: Eigenvectors must be nonzero, but an eigenvalue can be zero — a zero eigenvalue means the matrix is not invertible.
An n-by-n matrix is diagonalizable exactly when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors.
Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are automatically linearly independent.

misconceptions.text: The zero vector is an eigenvector for every eigenvalue.
misconceptions.corrective: Eigenvectors are required to be nonzero — A0 = λ0 holds trivially and identifies nothing about the matrix.

misconceptions.text: A matrix with a zero eigenvalue is a zero matrix.
misconceptions.corrective: A zero eigenvalue only means some nonzero vector is sent to zero — the matrix is singular, not necessarily zero.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero; orthogonal and orthonormal bases make coordinates, projections, and distance computations simple because the basis directions do not interfere.

facts.text: Nonzero orthogonal vectors are automatically linearly independent.
The orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace is the closest point of the subspace to that vector.
The Gram-Schmidt process converts any independent set into an orthogonal (or orthonormal) set spanning the same subspace.

misconceptions.text: Orthogonal just means perpendicular lines in a picture.
misconceptions.corrective: Orthogonality is defined by the inner product being zero, which extends to functions and high-dimensional data where no picture exists.

misconceptions.text: Projection changes the subspace you project onto.
misconceptions.corrective: Projection maps points INTO the subspace; vectors already in the subspace are unchanged by it.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: The least-squares solution of an inconsistent system Ax = b is the vector x̂ minimizing the length of the residual b − Ax; it satisfies the normal equations AᵀAx̂ = Aᵀb and corresponds to projecting b onto the column space of A.

facts.text: Least squares finds the best approximate solution when Ax = b has no exact solution, as with overdetermined data-fitting systems.
Geometrically, Ax̂ is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A.
When the columns of A are linearly independent, AᵀA is invertible and the least-squares solution is unique.

misconceptions.text: Least squares finds an exact solution to the system.
misconceptions.corrective: It minimizes the residual; the fitted values Ax̂ generally differ from b — being closest is not being equal.

misconceptions.text: A best-fit line must pass through the data points.
misconceptions.corrective: The least-squares line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps and can miss every single data point.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: The singular value decomposition factors any m-by-n matrix as A = UΣVᵀ with orthogonal U and V and a diagonal Σ of nonnegative singular values; it exists for every matrix, square or not.

facts.text: Every matrix has an SVD, unlike eigendecompositions, which require the matrix to be square and diagonalizable.
The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA, listed in decreasing order.
Truncating the SVD to the largest k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation of the matrix, the basis of compression and noise reduction.

misconceptions.text: Singular values are the same as eigenvalues.
misconceptions.corrective: Singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of AᵀA and are never negative; for non-symmetric or non-square matrices the two notions differ.

misconceptions.text: SVD only works for square matrices.
misconceptions.corrective: The SVD exists for every rectangular matrix — that generality is exactly why it is used on data matrices.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: The rank of a matrix is the dimension of its column space (the number of pivot columns); the nullity is the dimension of its null space; for an m-by-n matrix, rank plus nullity equals n.

facts.text: Row rank equals column rank for every matrix.
The rank-nullity theorem says rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, the number of columns of A.
A square n-by-n matrix is invertible exactly when its rank is n, equivalently when its nullity is 0.

misconceptions.text: Rank is the number of nonzero entries or nonzero rows in the original matrix.
misconceptions.corrective: Rank counts pivots AFTER row reduction; a matrix full of nonzero entries can still have rank 1 if its rows are proportional.

misconceptions.text: A tall matrix with many rows has large rank.
misconceptions.corrective: Rank never exceeds the smaller of the row and column counts, and dependence among columns lowers it further.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)

definition.text: A change of basis re-expresses vectors and transformations in a new coordinate system: the transition matrix converts coordinates between bases, and matrices A and P⁻¹AP represent the same transformation in different bases.

facts.text: The columns of the change-of-coordinates matrix are the new basis vectors written in the old basis.
Similar matrices P⁻¹AP and A share determinant, rank, characteristic polynomial, and eigenvalues.
Choosing an eigenvector basis, when one exists, makes a transformation's matrix diagonal — the point of diagonalization.

misconceptions.text: Changing basis changes the vector itself.
misconceptions.corrective: The vector is unchanged; only its coordinate description changes — like the same location under two different map grids.

misconceptions.text: Similar matrices are equal.
misconceptions.corrective: Similar matrices represent the same transformation in different bases and share invariants, but their entries generally differ.

attribution: Curated consensus linear algebra content; cross-checked against open texts (Hefferon, Linear Algebra; Beezer, A First Course in Linear Algebra)
